text: In 1928, the Woodlawn Property Owners Association organized a racially restrictive covenant in the northwest part of Woodlawn, a legal agreement among white owners not to sell or rent to Black buyers.
The university backed it, quietly, with lawyers and money.
From 1933 to 1947, the University of Chicago spent more than a hundred and ten thousand dollars on what it called community interests.
More than eighty-three thousand of that went to defending and enforcing restrictive covenants in Hyde Park, Washington Park, and Woodlawn.
Many of the restricted properties belonged to the university itself.
It tried to keep its name off the covenants in public, but the connection was no secret.
In 1937, an editorial in the Chicago Defender, the city's great Black newspaper, called those agreements the University of Chicago Agreement to get rid of Negroes.
The president through these years was Robert Maynard Hutchins, who led the university from 1929.
The Black attorney Earl B.
Dickerson, one of the law school's first Black graduates, went to Hutchins with two other lawyers and asked him to stop the university from backing the covenants.
By their account, Hutchins answered that he could not allow Black residents near the university because it would hurt enrollment.
Then in 1948, the United States Supreme Court ruled in Shelley versus Kraemer that courts could no longer enforce racial covenants.
The agreements stayed in the property records, but they lost their teeth.
So the same dollars that raised the limestone towers, the same institution that hired the stars and carved the gargoyles, also paid lawyers to keep a line drawn around the campus.
The Gothic quads looked like Oxford.
The thing they were protecting was something much closer to home.
That word, protected, the one people used for Hyde Park's parks and its lake and its university, would carry that second meaning for a long time to come.
The towers are still here.
The carved stone is still here.
And so is the question the carving was meant to answer, namely who the neighborhood was built for, and who it was built to keep out.
